domain: Political Linguistics / State Formation / Commitment Systems
topic_summary: Analysis of Turkey's 1928 alphabet reform (Law 1353), which replaced Arabic script with Latin script via top-down state imposition. The reform had effectively zero prior practitioners of Latin-script Turkish and was implemented within months, testing whether a commitment system kernel can be installed with no pre-existing occupancy of the new reading.

key_entities: Mustafa Kemal Atatürk (state authority; reform architect)
Ottoman Turkish literate class (Arabic-script practitioners; displaced)
Turkish Grand National Assembly (legislative body; Law 1353 passage)
key_tensions: State modernization imperative vs orthographic continuity (Kemalist state vs Ottoman tradition)
Literacy expansion vs cultural rupture (reformers vs traditional elites)
Imposed uniformity vs organic linguistic evolution (top-down vs bottom-up change)
key_mechanisms: Legislative prohibition: Arabic script banned in public documents, education, publishing
Mass literacy campaigns: Nation Schools (Millet Mektepleri) teaching Latin script to adults
Institutional enforcement: State employment, education access contingent on Latin-script literacy
key_absences: No documented resistance movements or alternative script proposals that gained institutional traction
Limited data on rural literacy rates pre/post reform to validate claimed literacy expansion

axes.human_readable: Orthographic Kernel Replacement (Script as Commitment System)
axes.structural_delta: Replacement of one orthographic kernel (Arabic script) with another (Latin script) as the fixed reference for legitimate written Turkish
axes.primary_observable: Legal status of scripts; institutional enforcement mechanisms; literacy curriculum content
axes.selection_reason: Core contested kernel; zero prior occupancy of Latin reading tests M-set gap hypothesis

axes.human_readable: State Capacity Expansion (Literacy as Legibility Mechanism)
axes.structural_delta: Alphabet reform as mechanism to expand state legibility and administrative reach via standardized literacy
axes.primary_observable: Literacy rates pre/post reform; state employment literacy requirements; census/taxation data quality
axes.selection_reason: Distinct observable (administrative capacity vs orthographic legitimacy); downstream synthesis of kernel effects

omegas.description: Does zero prior occupancy of Latin reading invalidate M-set continuity assumption? If kernel installation requires no pre-existing practitioners, the M-set may be a post-hoc rationalization rather than a structural constraint.

Claimed literacy expansion (3% to 33% by 1950s) lacks granular rural/urban breakdown. If gains concentrated in urban centers already targeted by state, reform may be Piton (state capacity) rather than Mountain (literacy barrier).

No documented organized resistance to script change. Does absence indicate genuine consensus, successful suppression, or historiographic gap? If suppression, continuity_reading may have higher ε than observable data suggests.

Iran and Arab states retained Arabic script despite similar modernization pressures. Does Turkish exceptionalism indicate unique state capacity (Rope) or unique cultural rupture willingness (Snare for tradition)?

fracture_scan.notes: No fractures detected. Kernel decomposition applied per §1.3-K. M-set gap hypothesis flagged as omega_m_set_gap for generation-stage testing.

commitment_system_recognition.kernel_description: Orthographic standard for written Turkish — the fixed script system that grounds legitimate literacy, state documentation, and cultural transmission
commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: State legislative and educational apparatus; legitimacy grounded in modernization imperative and national sovereignty claims

readings.commitment: Arabic script preserves Ottoman cultural continuity and Islamic textual tradition
readings.authority_grounding: Traditional religious and literary elites; legitimacy from historical precedent
readings.expected_structural_delta: High ε for Ottoman literate class (victim set); low ε for state modernization (blocked reform path)

readings.commitment: Latin script enables technological/scientific modernization while preserving Turkish linguistic identity
readings.authority_grounding: Kemalist state; legitimacy from national sovereignty and European alignment
readings.expected_structural_delta: Moderate ε (literacy expansion costs); beneficiary set = state bureaucracy + new literate class

readings.commitment: Script change as deliberate cultural rupture to sever Ottoman/Islamic past and create new national identity
readings.authority_grounding: Radical Kemalist faction; legitimacy from revolutionary transformation mandate
readings.expected_structural_delta: Very high ε for cultural continuity (victim set = entire pre-reform literate population); beneficiary set = post-reform state apparatus

axiom_contradictions.basis: Continuity reading holds that orthographic stability is necessary for cultural transmission; rupture reading holds that orthographic discontinuity is necessary for cultural transformation. No coherent framework can simultaneously require stability and discontinuity of the same substrate.

Continuity reading grounds legitimacy in historical precedent and religious tradition; modernization reading grounds legitimacy in technological efficiency and European alignment. These are mutually exclusive sources of orthographic authority.
